segment.text: 武者修行としても一種特別の願望を以て江戸を出たので有った。疾くに目的を達して今頃は江戸に帰り、喜ぶ恩師の顔を見て、一家相伝の極意秘伝を停滞なく受けていなければ成らぬのが、意外な支障に引掛って、三月余りを殆ど囚虜の身に均しく過ごしたのであった。

sentences.text: 武者修行としても一種特別の願望を以て江戸を出たので有った。
疾くに目的を達して今頃は江戸に帰り、喜ぶ恩師の顔を見て、一家相伝の極意秘伝を停滞なく受けていなければ成らぬのが、意外な支障に引掛って、三月余りを殆ど囚虜の身に均しく過ごしたのであった。

segment.text: 常陸の国、河内郡、阿波村の大杉明神の近くに、恐しい妖魔が住んでいるので有った。それに竜次郎は捕って、水鳥が霞網に搦ったも同然、如何とも仕難くなったのであった。一と夏を其妖魔の家に心成らずも日を過して、今朝の秋とは成ったので有った。

segment.text: とは知らぬ磯貝竜次郎、武者修行に出て利根の夜船に乗った時に、江戸帰りのお鉄と一緒で有った。年齢は既に四十近く、姥桜も散り過ぎた大年増。重量は二十貫の上もあろう程の肥満した体。色は浅黒く、髪の毛には波を打ったような癖が目立って、若も生端薄く、それを無造作に何時も櫛巻きにしていた。鼻は低く、口は大きく、腮は二重に見えるので有ったが、如何にも其眼元に愛嬌が溢れていた。然うして云う事為る事、如才無く、総てがきびきびとして気が利いていた。若い時には斯うした風のが、却って男の心を動かしたかも知れぬのだ。

sentences.text: とは知らぬ磯貝竜次郎、武者修行に出て利根の夜船に乗った時に、江戸帰りのお鉄と一緒で有った。
年齢は既に四十近く、姥桜も散り過ぎた大年増。
重量は二十貫の上もあろう程の肥満した体。
色は浅黒く、髪の毛には波を打ったような癖が目立って、若も生端薄く、それを無造作に何時も櫛巻きにしていた。
鼻は低く、口は大きく、腮は二重に見えるので有ったが、如何にも其眼元に愛嬌が溢れていた。
然うして云う事為る事、如才無く、総てがきびきびとして気が利いていた。
若い時には斯うした風のが、却って男の心を動かしたかも知れぬのだ。

segment.text: 「此間の夜も。しみじみ云いました通り、私が以前に水戸の藤田先生の御存命中に承わった処では、今に世の中がどんでん返しをして、吃驚する程変ってくる。だから武家も、別して旗本衆などは、余程考えていなければ成らないので、大概なら剣道とか槍術とか、そんな方は見切りをつけて、砲術を学んだ方が為に成る。それには一度毛唐人の国へ行って来た方が好いとのお話……私は、実は貴郎に、米利堅へでも、和蘭陀へでも渡航して頂きたい位に考えて居りますのです。失礼ながら金は祖父の代から溜め込んで有るんですからね。二千や三千の金なら、何時でも耳が揃えられるんです」

sentences.text: 「此間の夜も。
しみじみ云いました通り、私が以前に水戸の藤田先生の御存命中に承わった処では、今に世の中がどんでん返しをして、吃驚する程変ってくる。
だから武家も、別して旗本衆などは、余程考えていなければ成らないので、大概なら剣道とか槍術とか、そんな方は見切りをつけて、砲術を学んだ方が為に成る。
それには一度毛唐人の国へ行って来た方が好いとのお話……私は、実は貴郎に、米利堅へでも、和蘭陀へでも渡航して頂きたい位に考えて居りますのです。
失礼ながら金は祖父の代から溜め込んで有るんですからね。
二千や三千の金なら、何時でも耳が揃えられるんです」

segment.text: 師の陣風斎という人は、実際轗軻不遇の士。考えれば考える程気の毒で成らなかった。斎藤弥九郎、千葉周作、桃井春蔵、それ等の剣道師範に比べて、敢て腕前は劣らぬのだ。けれど他が何千という弟子を取り、幕府或は諸侯から後援せられているに関らず、秋岡陣風斎は浪宅に貧窮の生活をつづけていて、弟子と云っては実に自分一人だ。其処が併し偉い点だ。わざと然うした運命に身を潜めたのかも知れないのだが、何んにしても其恩には、充分報じなければ成らないのだ。

segment.text: 此所の渡しというのは、別に渡し守がいるのではなく、船だけ備えて有るばかりで、世に云う手繰り渡しに成っているのだ。それは両岸に高く材木を三本組合せて立て、それに藤蔓を綯って引張って置き、それに小さな針鉄の輪を箝めて、其輪に綱を結んで、田船の舳に繋いで有るのだ。田船の舳と艫とには、又別に麻縄が長く結付けてあって、どちらも両方の岸にまで届く程の長さがある。つまり田船の中に乗った者が、自分で舳の縄を手繰れば、向岸へ着く。其後へ又来た者が、其空船を此方へ呼戻す時には、岸から艫の縄を手繰ると、人は無くても船は房って来る、然ういう甚だ元始的の方法で有った。

segment.text: 悪僧は再び手桶を提げて、蘆の間に忽然と姿を隠した。何んという無慈悲な坊主だろう。人を助ける出家の身が、鰻掻きをして殺生戒を破るさえ無茶苦茶なのに、彼岸に達する救世の船。それを取上げて了ったので有った。一体何寺の何んという坊主だろう。憎さも憎しと竜次郎は、歯軋りをして口惜しがった。併し新利根川の堀割を隔てているのて、如何する事も出来なかった。

segment.text: 普通の者には出来ぬ芸だが、女軽業師の小虎としては、何んの造作も無いので有った。一座を脱出する時に、変り易い秋の空を気遣って、手当り次第に雨傘を持出したのが、図らず此所で役に立った。太夫身支度の間今一囃子、そんな景気を附けるでもなく、唯浴衣の裾を端折っただけで有った。赤の色褪めた唐縮緬の腰巻が、新堀割の濁った水の色や、小堤下の泥の色に反映して、意外に美しく引立って見えるので有った。

segment.text: 折柄の夕陽は横斜に小虎の半身を赤々と照らした。それが流れの鈍い水の面にも写るので有った。上にも小虎、下にも小虎、一人が二人に割れて見えた。垢染みた浴衣の扮装も、斯うすると光輝を放って見えるので有った。況してや舞台好みの文金高島田、化粧をした顔の美艶、竜次郎は恍惚たらざるを得なかった。もう途中で落ちはせぬかという懸念は無く成ったが、あの儘自分だけで渡り終って、先を急ぐとて独で行って了いはせぬか。それが気遣われるばかりで有った。

segment.text: やがて其半途まで綱渡りを進めた。両岸からは如何に高く藤蔓を張っても、其中心に当る点は、自然々々にたるみが出来て水面近く垂れているので有った。それに人の身の重量が加わったので、危く水に漬りそうにまで成った。それすら小虎は巧みに越した。もう其難場は越したので、一息吐くかと思う頃。

chapter_summaries.0: 一: Ryūjirō readies to flee. Set-up: hatamoto swordsman on shrine-purification pilgrimage for Happō Makigumo transmission, beached three months at Awa by Living-Rope O-Tetsu, widowed oyabun with 1000 kobun and rumoured torture-murders of five-six men. Portrait of fortyish corpulent O-Tetsu; carrying on back, nursing, invisible sickness, decision to slip via back cliff to Fukuda.

hard_spots.why_hard: Two-paragraph incantatory list of rope arts (kakenawa, toinawa, hikinawa etc.) and holds (ganjigarame, kikkō, matsuba, rokuro-maki, takade, kote...) plus sō-returns in shin-gyō-sō variants. Tempts summarising; must be kept at full length because p164 later binds Ryūjirō 'exactly like a ganjigarame'. Requires consistent English set, not varied synonyms.

Full-paragraph kōdan explanation of hand-hauled ferry: tripods, creeper cable, iron ring, bow/stern hemp lines. Narrator pauses to savour it and adds donated retired capture-ropes from Hōzōji hemp. Do not move to footnote or compress into efficient summary.

Single-speech village rumour listing five-six dead captives with kirishitan-bateren joke and evil-eye paralysis. Delivers O-Tetsu's menace as hearsay, not fact. Keep as reported speech, not settled history.
Narrator's lecture that before telegraph/telephone/post, bad dreams and broken sandal-thongs were reason to cross provinces. Pulp sociology that licenses both escapes. Do not shrink to a sentence.

Sour-smelling cooled water and chopped surume lunch as possible poisoning. Text offers as retrospective evil surmise (邪推), never confirmed. English must keep as suspicion, not fact that O-Tetsu drugged him.

Rope biting into O-Tetsu's rich flesh as she slips free; faded red crepe loincloth against muddy water; blood-spray that is only red dragonflies. Linger at original level: neither veiled nor heated up.

Kozuka thrown 50 ken into monk's brow; Kotora's sudden side-stab of O-Tetsu, one scream, knife wiped on sleeve and returned. No remorse build-up, no confirmed death statement. Keep breath-short and deadpan.

Leap to mid-Meiji: famous First detective printed as circles ○○○○○ as Ryūjirō's later self, Kotora as dead first wife, and flat shrug whether Happō Makigumo secret was ever transmitted. Keep circles and shrug; do not explain or resolve.

motifs.english: Keep one audible web: rope / cord / vine / line / bind / tie / fasten / entangle / coil / haul / cut loose / slip free. Do not vary for elegance. Technical holds keep same English each time.

narration.english_tense: Past for narrated action (de-aru / -ta habits rendered as simple past); keep present only where narrator steps forward to explain custom or mechanism in general truth
narration.frame: Third-person popular-Taishō kōdan narration in formal de-aru style with frequent stepping-forward: rumour speech, how-things-work lectures, dream sociology, half-century leap to Meiji coda. Nine titled sections (一–九) plus asterisk break and flat epilogue.
narration.narrator: Extra-diegetic kōdan storyteller who knows rumour, rope lore, ferry gear and postal history and performs them in voice; straight-faced, digressive, anticlimactic
narration.tense_habits: Literary de-aru / -tari past narration with mid-paragraph gnomic asides; dreams and rumour in reported present; dialogue in period Edo speech. Do not normalise shifts or tidy chronology.
timeline: Edo departure for musha-shugyō + shrine purification circuit (Katori-Kashima-Ikisu, Nagareyama Suwa, Awa Ōsugi, Tatsuki Mizuchi)
Night boat via Tone, sour yuhashi + surume lunch; carried half-ri by O-Tetsu to Awa house
Three months luxurious captivity (summer into early autumn): midnight rope lessons, invisible rope, thrown-rope recapture
Escape in O-Tetsu's absence; afternoon meeting with Kotora fugitive from Edosaki via back roads
Shin-Tone ferry blockage, tightrope attempt, creeper cut, weed struggle, naked robbery at dusk
O-Tetsu reveal, stab, walk toward Edo; coda leap to mid-Meiji detective and unknown transmission

Set-up: hatamoto swordsman on shrine-purification pilgrimage for Happō Makigumo transmission, beached three months at Awa by Living-Rope O-Tetsu, widowed oyabun with 1000 kobun and rumoured torture-murders of five-six men. Portrait of fortyish corpulent O-Tetsu; carrying on back, nursing, invisible sickness, decision to slip via back cliff to Fukuda.

二: Conscience and backstory. Training under Imahori and sole pupil of rōnin Akioka Jinpūsai; pilgrimage order to shrines. Poison suspicion (surume, sour yuhashi). Hereditary mekashi house; midnight rope-lesson catalogue (holds and shin-gyō-sō variants), mutual tying, O-Tetsu slipping bonds. Flattered as house swordsman better than Hirate Miki; thrown-rope recapture from cliff.

三: Recapture and bargaining. Hog-tied in back upstairs while O-Tetsu drinks. Ryūjirō invents/ reports nightly dream of dying kinless master; pleads one Edo nursing visit on oath to return. O-Tetsu releases and strokes rope-marks, extracts promises: foreign gunnery voyage on hoarded thousands, and jealous ban on other women. Jealousy as stored bulk.

四: Send-off and new companion. O-Tetsu kits him out (michiyuki, tsuka-bukuro, tekko-kyahan) and warns kobun everywhere. Ryūjirō hurries via Fukuda-Ichizaki toward Fūkawa-Fussa-Abiko. Meets incongruous beauty: high coiffure and heavy makeup with shabby dyed yukata and rain umbrella, bare feet. She shadows him; both claim night road for sick masters.

五: Dream essay and Kotora's tale. Narrator lectures that without telegraph/post a bad dream justified crossing provinces. Girl is Take-wari Kotora, foundling of grand-master Toradayū (now paralysed in Honjo), fleeing miserly Toramatsu from Edosaki engagement. They hurry for Hontone crossing before dark; reach lonely Shin-Tone hand-hauled ferry and begin hauling.

六: Ferry blocked. Giant fallen monk (earth-coloured nasshogi, twisted headband, sword scar) hauls opposite rope one-handed, wins tug, stern line snaps. He jeers, hides for eels. Kotora offers tightrope on creeper via umbrella; red loincloth flash, dragonflies like blood-spray, sunset double on water. Midway creeper snaps; she falls with loud splash.

七: Water rescue. Monk reappears with eel-knife, boasts he cut vine, taunts about man-eating weeds/algae. Kotora swims then is seized hand-foot-side-shoulder like living hands. Ryūjirō throws kozuka 50 ken into monk's brow, strips to tekko-kyahan and loincloth dirk, swims, finds weeds like ganjigarame, cuts free with O-Tetsu's rope-cutting method.

八: Naked robbery. Ryūjirō cuts weeds one-handed while guarding blade near Kotora, swims back to same bank. Leeches mistaken for knife wounds. Clothes, two swords, pocket things, towel and nose-paper gone. Farmhouses refuse lodging at night rule. They return to ferry under evening moon; Ryūjirō tells Kotora go on alone; she refuses, offers belly-band savings for secondhand clothes in Fūkawa.

九 + coda: O-Tetsu springs from reeds, owns theft via forward net of kobun, reveals monk as old kobun Ahodara Gonji and farmers silenced. Jealous rage beats and spits on Kotora. Ryūjirō gives up Edo trip to prove innocence; while mother-dressing him she is side-stabbed by Kotora with his dirk — one scream, woman's pride, knife wiped and returned. Asterisks: Ryūjirō as Meiji's First detective ○○○○○, Kotora dead first wife; whether secret transmitted unknown.

body.say: Rope is plot, not colour: keep catalogues full and binding-words literal; keep hero passive, O-Tetsu unglamorous-menacing, Kotora polite then abrupt, ending flat. Where passage contradicts this bible, passage wins — say so.

style_sheet.annotation_density: Sparse, for what sentence cannot give: torinawa arts, jitte / aka-fusa, Shin-Tone / Hontone geography, kirishitan-bateren joke, Mito prophecy, circles redaction. Never for what context supplies. Margin explains choices; text wins over reader ease.
style_sheet.author_voice: Brisk magazine kōdan under bookish Sinitic ornament: formal de-aru narration, performed rumour, lingering erotic-comic body description, deadpan anticlimax. Neither faux-Edo pastiche nor sleek modern flat. Keep scale comedy (carried like child, dressed after bath) and failing body (pallor, sunken eyes, grown topknot) plain.
style_sheet.honorifics_and_names: Japanese order surname-first; macrons (Ryūjirō, Jinpūsai, Toradayū). Keep Sensei for Akioka where pupil-duty weight matters; keep O- prefix (O-Tetsu, not Tetsu). 先生 addressed to Ryūjirō as 'Sensei' to keep house-swordsman irony. Danna-sama for Kotora's address. No -san/-sama beyond what English needs.
style_sheet.keep_in_japanese: Sensei, hatamoto, kobun, jitte, torinawa/kakenawa etc. with first-use gloss; place-names in romanisation (Awa, Shin-Tone, Tatsuki). Named holds in consistent English with Japanese first time (e.g. ganjigarame cross-lattice bind) then English alone.
style_sheet.quotation: Dialogue in double quotes; rumour speech and reported injunctions as quoted blocks where original sets them as performance. Keep who-said-what spare as original leaves it.
style_sheet.register: Narration literate-formal but brisk; dialogue sharply differentiated: Ryūjirō samurai-formal self-abasing, O-Tetsu cajoling-commanding-jealous, Kotora polite-feminine snapping to vulgar then flat, monk music-hall vulgar.
style_sheet.ruby_and_italics: Ruby readings (e.g. 磯貝竜次郎いそがいりゅうじろう) do not appear in English; use romanised name. Italics only for coda circles ○○○○○ and for blood-spray/dragonfly feint if needed. No italics for Japanese terms after first gloss.

english: A samurai's soul. With only the paired long and short swords at his waist, with no time to take anything in his hands and barely time to shove his feet into his sandals, Isogai Ryujiro stepped out into the back garden.
"Come what may, today I shall make up my mind and leave."

He had left Edo on a warrior pilgrimage, but with a wish of a rather special kind. He should long since have gained his end and be back in Edo by now, looking on the joyful face of his honoured master and receiving without delay the secret transmission handed down in his house alone. Instead he had been caught on an unforeseen snag and had spent more than three months living all but a prisoner.

In the province of Hitachi, in Kochi district, near the Osugi Shrine in Awa village, there lived a fearsome demon. Ryujiro had been caught by it, no different from a water bird tangled in a mist net, and could do nothing about it. Against his will he had spent a whole summer in that demon's house, and this morning it was autumn.
The Osugi Shrine is said to enshrine Hitachi-bo Kaison, in common speech the rough god of the tengu. Nearby there was a demon of great renown. She was the woman boss called Living-Rope O-Tetsu.

Of course, being the country, there was something countrified about it all, but all the same her territory straddled Hitachi and Shimosa across the River Tone, and her kobun numbered a full thousand with nothing discounted. O-Tetsu's husband, Hiwatari Jinemon, was a police informer entrusted by the authorities with a red-tasselled jitte and capture-ropes, and he wore two pairs of straw sandals at once. He was a sworn brother to Ioka no Sukegoro.

Though that Hiwatari Jinemon had died of sickness, his widow O-Tetsu was more than a match for a man, for all the world like a woman informer herself, so that people feared and dreaded her as if she still held the red-tasselled jitte.
takes.label: a. brisk kōdan storyteller (recommended first)
takes.line: Narration: a confident popular storyteller in clean, slightly formal English, happy to pause for a rope catalogue or a ferry mechanism and to deliver the Meiji coda with a straight face; pace brisk under the ornament, no archaism. Ryūjirō speaks careful, self-deprecating samurai politeness even when begging; O-Tetsu is warm, cajoling and peremptory in one breath, a boss used to obedience, coarsening as jealousy rises; Kotora is sweetly formal until she isn't; the monk is pure vulgar bluster. Wrong for it: lyrical ennoblement, hard-boiled modern slang, or any hint of parody — the storyteller believes every word.

english: The soul of the samurai. With only his two swords, long and short, at his waist, nothing in his hands, and his sandals barely thrust on, Isogai Ryujiro stepped out into the back yard.
"Whatever may happen, today I will make up my mind and be gone."

He had left Edo on a warrior pilgrimage with a wish of a rather special kind. He should long since have gained his end and be back in Edo by now, looking upon the glad face of his master and receiving without hindrance the innermost secret handed down in a single house. Instead he had been caught by an unforeseen hindrance and had spent more than three months all but a prisoner.

In the province of Hitachi, in Kochi district, near the Osugi Myojin of Awa village, there lived a fearful demon. Ryujiro had been caught by it, no different from a water bird tangled in a mist net, and there was nothing to be done. Against his will he had spent a whole summer in that demon's house, and this morning it had become autumn.
The Osugi Myojin is said to enshrine Hitachibo Kaison, in common speech the tengu war god. Near it there lived a notorious monster of the place. She was O-Tetsu the Living Rope, a woman boss.

Country business, of course, and coarse with the mud of the fields, but her territory straddled Hitachi and Shimosa across the Tone River, and of kobun followers she could muster a full thousand. O-Tetsu's husband, Hiwatari Jinemon, was a police agent entrusted by the authorities with a red-tasselled jitte truncheon and capture ropes, and he wore two pairs of straw sandals at once. He was sworn brother to Sukegoro of Ioka.
Though Hiwatari Jinemon had died of sickness, his widow O-Tetsu was more manly than any man, all but a woman agent herself, so that people feared her still as if she yet held the red-tasselled jitte.
takes.label: b. drier and more deadpan
takes.line: Narration: the same events in plainer, cooler sentences, letting the humiliations and the sudden stab land without emphasis; explanations kept but trimmed of relish. Speakers differ mainly by bluntness: Ryūjirō meeker, O-Tetsu flatter and therefore more frightening, Kotora matter-of-fact about murder. Wrong for it: it risks reading as modern irony about pulp rather than pulp; use only if the house wants the anticlimax underlined.

Country business it was, to be sure, and earthy with it, but nonetheless her ground straddled Hitachi and Shimosa across the Tone River, and of kobun followers she could muster a full thousand, second to none. takes.label: c. fuller period melodrama
takes.line: Narration: warmer, more rolling and openly sentimental, leaning into the tearful plea scene, the sunset doubling Kotora on the water, and the rhetoric of master-and-disciple devotion; dialogue more expansive, O-Tetsu's jealousy played at full tragic volume. Wrong for it: it can swell into the very ennoblement the text warns against and slow the kōdan pace; the murder and the shrugging coda would need deliberate flattening to survive it.

options.author: the first read (Wonder)
options.case: - The story stands or falls on its title made literal: the sword fails and the rope, in every form, does everything. Ryūjirō's great sword, the 'soul of the samurai', is stolen off a riverbank while he is naked; his small knife is useful only once, thrown at a man and then used as a weed-cutter. What actually saves a life, twice, is the low, female, criminal-adjacent art he learned in captivity from O-Tetsu: rope-escape and rope-cutting, applied underwater to the man-eating weeds that hold Kotora. Around that core the text binds everything to everything else — the invisible rope that keeps him in Awa for three months, the thrown rope that fishes him off the cliff, the ferry's hauling-ropes (themselves donated, used-up capture-ropes, a detail the narrator pauses to savour), the weeds that climb his body 'like a real rope-hold', the jealousy that is also a kind of tying. A translation that treats the rope business as colour, cuts the catalogues, or lets the swordsmanship reassert heroic dignity has lost the book's actual engine, which is a proud hatamoto swordsman being progressively stripped — of movement, of clothes, of his sword, of initiative — and rescued, bound, dressed and finally freed by women. Because the plot is built as a chain of bindings and releases, and because Ryūjirō's passivity is the point, not a flaw to be tidied. He is carried on O-Tetsu's back, nursed, kept, flattered as a house swordsman 'better than Hirate Mikizō', caught mid-escape like a fish on a line; he apologises, weeps, promises, undresses, and is dressed again by O-Tetsu 'like a mother after a child's bath'. Kotora walks the rope he cannot, swims, is cut free by his borrowed skill, and then settles the whole impasse in one stab while he stands by astonished at fate. If the English lets him sound decisive or lets O-Tetsu become a glamorous villainess, the humiliation-comedy and the real menace both go. For the English: Keep the ropes literal. Give the named holds and techniques in a consistent, recognisable set of English terms, and let the catalogue run at its full, slightly excessive length the first time: it is plot, not ornament, because the algae will later bind him 'exactly like a ganjigarame hold'. Do not vary rope, bind, tie, entangle, prisoner for elegance; the text's network of repeated binding-words is its structure, and flattening it is destroying that network.
options.tradeoff: One tightly focused crux: the rope-binds, sword-fails chain and Ryūjirō's consequential passivity.

options.author: the crux check (Wonder)
options.case:
- The whole story is organised by rope displacing the sword, literally and metaphorically — this is what the title announces and what every episode re-enacts. Otetsu is Ikina wa, 'Living Rope': a bondage/arrest-rope (torinawa) expert whose house transmits knot-lists (ganjigarame, kikkou, matsuba, rokuro…) that Ryuujirou studies by being tied and tying her in midnight lessons. He is then held three months by an 'invisible rope' though never locked in, is hauled back by her thrown rope when he escapes, crosses paths with the ferry's hauling-ropes (made, pointedly, from retired arrest-ropes), watches Kotora tightrope the ferry vine, is nearly drowned by man-eating algae that binds him 'like a ganjigarame', and frees himself and her only by applying Otetsu's rope-escape/rope-cutting teaching with his small knife. Even Otetsu's jealous surveillance is described as a net spread along the road. Against this, the samurai's daishou do nothing: the long sword is left on the bank and stolen, and the only blades that work are the kozuka thrown at the monk and the kodachi cutting weeds in the water. For the English: Keep one audible lexical web — rope, cord, bind, tie, tangle, coil, haul, cut loose, escape — recurring even where idiomatic English would vary it, and keep the technical catalogues of knots and holds at full, incantatory length. Likewise let the swords stay inert: never drawn in combat, finally stolen while he is naked; do not heroicise Ryuujirou into a swordsman in action.
- The ending's moral and narrative abruptness is deliberate pulp mechanics, not a flaw to be repaired: the captive's problem is 'solved' by a near-stranger's sudden murder, and the frame then leaps to Meiji and openly admits it doesn't know the outcome that mattered most. Otetsu is simultaneously rumoured torturer-murderer of five or six men, tender nurse, would-be financier of a forward-looking future (sending Ryuujirou to America or Holland to learn gunnery, having heard Fujita in Mito predict the world overturned), infantilising captor, and pathologically jealous wife-figure. Ryuujirou is a 500-koku hatamoto swordsman of reputed genius who spends the tale sick, bound, carried, stripped and rescued. Kotora, met that afternoon, stabs Otetsu in the side without warning — 'a woman's pride' — hands back the wiped blade, and the narrative declares the insoluble problem simply settled; three asterisks later Ryuujirou is a famous Meiji police detective, Kotora his dead first wife, and whether he ever received the Happou Makigumo secret 'regrettably is not transmitted.' For the English: Preserve the sensational, deadpan narration and its refusals: do not clarify who is villain or victim, do not soften the bondage's erotic charge or the jealous violence, do not give the stabbing a moral build-up it doesn't have, and do not fill the epilogue's gap about the secret transmission. Where a fluent version would explain or resolve, leave the seam showing.
options.tradeoff: The same rope-displaces-sword crux plus a second, independent one: the deliberate pulp abruptness and unresolved refusals of the ending.

fork.question: Do the two readings name the same crux in different words, or different cruxes? They agree on the rope-displaces-sword structure, but Option 1 adds a second crux — preserving the ending's sudden murder, deadpan non-resolution and the epilogue's admitted gap — which would govern different margin decisions from Option 0's binding-and-passivity crux alone, so the run cannot treat them as interchangeable statements of one reading without an editor ruling on whether the translation stands or falls on one thing or on two.

head.reason: Fork opened because the first parts do name the same rope-over-sword structure, but Option 1 names a materially different second crux about pulp abruptness and refusal to resolve, which Option 0 does not; that difference will drive recurring choices about clarification, moral build-up and the epilogue, and getting its status wrong would be expensive across the text.
head.say: I recommend we proceed on Option 1 until the editor rules: it preserves the shared rope-displaces-sword finding as written and gives the run an explicit guard against clarifying or resolving the ending, whereas proceeding on Option 0 alone risks letting fluent tidying repair precisely the seams Option 1 identifies; the editor should rule whether that abruptness is a second, co-equal crux or a consequence to be handled under the first.
