The Osugi Shrine is said to enshrine Hitachi-bo Kaison, in common speech the rough god of the tengu. Nearby there was a demon of great renown. She was the woman boss called Living-Rope O-Tetsu.
notes: Chose Living-Rope for ikinawa to keep title-word literal from first appearance.

payload.english: Of course, being the country, there was something countrified about it all, but all the same her territory straddled Hitachi and Shimosa across the River Tone, and her kobun numbered a full thousand with nothing discounted. O-Tetsu's husband, Hiwatari Jinemon, was a police informer entrusted by the authorities with a red-tasselled jitte and capture-ropes, and he wore two pairs of straw sandals at once. He was a sworn brother to Ioka no Sukegoro.
notes: Left kobun, jitte and two pairs of sandals literal; reader can take double life from context.

payload.english: Though that Hiwatari Jinemon had died of sickness, his widow O-Tetsu was more than a match for a man, for all the world like a woman informer herself, so that people feared and dreaded her as if she still held the red-tasselled jitte.

payload.say: Drafted the rumour set piece and O-Tetsu portrait keeping hearsay, catalogue of victims, and physical appraisal literal.

payload.english: "Living-Rope O-Tetsu is the best in the land at taking men. Once she takes you, you are done for. Guilty or not does not come into it. By some torture strange to this world, she must have killed five or six by now. Arashi Hinamaru, the travelling player who came to the market at Awa, was killed. The young fellow selling Echigo chijimi was killed. Then the travelling painter from Kyoto and the journeyman carpenter from Odawara. The second son of the makomo magnate of Ukishima was caught too, but none of them lasted three months. Is that what they call the deep love of a wicked woman. She can hardly be a Kirishitan bateren priest, but they say one short glare from those eyes leaves the body numb and helpless."
notes: Kept as performed rumour speech, not settled fact. Left Kirishitan bateren unglossed for the margin. Kept five or six and three months literal.

payload.english: Talk like this stood everywhere.

Knowing none of this, Isogai Ryujiro set out on his warrior pilgrimage, boarded the night boat on the Tone, and found himself together with O-Tetsu, on her way back from Edo. She was already close to forty, an older woman well past the late cherry bloom. A stout body that must have weighed over twenty kan. Her colour dark, her hair showing a marked wavy quirk and thin at the temples, which she always wore twisted up carelessly with a comb. Low nose, large mouth, a chin that looked double, and yet about her eyes there was an overflowing charm. Everything she said and did was deft, brisk in every way and full of tact. In her youth, a woman of just this sort might rather have moved a man's heart.
notes: Kept twenty kan as a measure and the appraisal flat as written, neither leering nor rescuing. Rendered ubazakura literally as late cherry bloom.

payload.english: "If you are going to worship at Osugi-sama, you must stop by at our house."

payload.say: Drafted p13 to p18 in the brisk kodan voice, keeping prisoner and demon consistent with the opening.

payload.english: Coming up on the night boat at Oshisuna-gashi, on the reed plain on the way to Awa village, when Ryujiro was suddenly seized with pain in the belly, O-Tetsu picked him up on her back as lightly as if he had been a child, carried him home the not quite half a ri, and nursed him with a care no kin could have matched. That much was well enough, but then never to be allowed a single step outside was a nuisance beyond all bearing.

Ryujiro's pain was soon cured, but the health he had happily got back began to fail again in two or three days, and with nothing in particular amiss he spent his days in a lingering sickness, like a man with the stuffing taken out of him. His topknot stubble had grown out. His colour turned pale. His own sunken eyes startled him. He had become the demon's prisoner in very truth.
notes: Kept 'prisoner' to hold the book's binding-web: toriko here answers 'all but a prisoner' in p4.

payload.english: Today at last he had worked up his great resolve, and meaning to profit by O-Tetsu's absence to climb down the cliff from the back garden and make his way by the paddies toward Fukuda village.
II

With every step the pangs of conscience pressed harder. That Isogai Ryujiro, though a second son, born to a house of five hundred koku hatamoto, a direct retainer of the shogun, whose rare mastery of the sword was called heaven-born and rang through all the Kobusho, should for the sake of one woman, older than himself, of low standing, and of no great beauty, have been rolled in the palm of her hand and handled for three months like a plaything.

At the Kobusho he had studied chiefly under the guidance of Imahori Settsu-no-kami, but besides that he had won the favour of Akioka Jinpusai, who lived retired at Azabu Furukawabata and had opened a new line from the Tenshin Dokumei school, and had received separate training as his one master with his one pupil, until he had advanced to the place of inheriting the secret of the Happo Makigumo swordsmanship.
notes: Romanisation without macrons follows the house's chosen first page, against the bible's macrons, for consistency.

payload.english: "Before that transmission, you must without fail go out on a warrior pilgrimage and travel the provinces once. By that I do not mean for you to go breaking down the doors of ordinary training halls. First visit the three shrines of Katori, Kashima, and Ikisu, and then the Suwa shrine at Nagareyama, in Hitachi the Osugi shrine in Awa village and the Mizuchi shrine in Tatsuki village. Visit those gods, purify both body and mind together, wield and offer up the sacred sword in its full form, and come back having cast off all base intent. Visits to other gods may come afterward at your leisure."
notes: Master's injunction quoted as reported instruction; shrine circuit kept in full as the pilgrimage program whose interruption at Osugi drives the plot.

payload.english: To receive the Happo Makigumo swordsmanship from Akioka Jinpusai as his one master with his one pupil, Ryujiro's journey through the provinces had begun. But he had come to a halt at the Osugi shrine. However one looked at it, it could only be called strange.

Before landing at Oshisuna-gashi, he had bought a lunch sold early in the morning at Kioroshi-gashi. He could not think it was only the chopped dried squid in it disagreeing with him that had given him the stomach pain. Before that, when he had felt thirst in the closeness of the crowded boat, the cooled boiled water O-Tetsu gave him had something strange in its smell. To think evilly of it, he might have been made to drink some drug.
notes: Kept as retrospective suspicion, not fact: the text offers poison only as evil surmise.

payload.english: Once taken into O-Tetsu's house, his blood thickened, his sinews slackened, his spirit failed, and he was left helpless in every way. He only grew witless.

O-Tetsu's house were hereditary police agents. Her grandfather had been especially famed. Hiwatari Jinemon was an adopted husband. For that reason O-Tetsu herself was the better versed in matters of arrest.
"When it comes to laying a capture-rope, there is none in Hitachi, Shimosa, or Kazusa to match me."
notes: First full claim of rope mastery; capture-rope kept literal for torinawa network.

payload.say: Drafted the rope catalogue and midnight lessons at full length with a consistent set of holds.

payload.english: Her boast had more than enough strength behind it. Woman though she was, she was practiced in it all: kakenawa laying-rope, nagenawa throwing-rope, hikinawa hauling-rope, tsurinawa fishing-rope, nukenawa slipping-rope. In ways of laying a capture-rope she knew every hold: the ganjigarame cross-lattice bind, the kikko tortoise-shell tie, the matsuba pine-needle cinch, the rokuro-maki windlass coil, high hands, low hands, single-hand lift, reverse knot.
notes: Kept the catalogue at full length without varying rope/bind/tie. Rope arts given as Japanese with English gloss on first use; holds given in the same set to be reused later, especially ganjigarame.

payload.english: Agemaki topknot, cross, diamond, crab, fish-scale, and each of those had its three ways, shin, gyo, and so, formal, running, and grass. The minute exposition of each school had come down in the house as written copies.
notes: Left shin-gyo-so as terms with plain gloss; did not compress the second list, as it is the same incantatory catalogue.

payload.english: Ryujiro took an interest in this capture-rope too, and to pass the boredom he read every copy that remained, and from there his wish to study only grew, and he learned the practice from O-Tetsu herself.

"This is handed down from one child alone to one child alone, but since it is you I will hand it down to you. Only it is strictly forbidden, no matter what, that I teach it by day, so I will teach you at midnight."
To teach, O-Tetsu worked the capture-rope and bound Ryujiro. And she let Ryujiro bind her too.
"The art of slipping rope is not for thieves alone. I think it is good for a samurai house to learn it too. When you are taken prisoner by the enemy, it will serve you."

Even the tight binding of the main rope biting into fat O-Tetsu's rich flesh, while she writhed and cut the wind with her shoulders and set waves running across her belly, became a fine slipping free into a free body. Ryujiro could not help marveling from the bottom of his heart.
notes: Kept the lingering at the original level, neither veiled nor heated: biting rope, shoulders, belly, slipping free.

payload.english: While this went on, Ryujiro felt as if he were bound at all times by an invisible rope and tied fast, and could not set a foot outside. O-Tetsu was almost never away from him and would not even let him worship at the nearby Osugi Shrine. When she had no choice but to go out, she had her kobun watch him.
notes: Kept invisible rope / bound / tied fast literal to hold the binding web; kept kobun per style sheet.

payload.english: In return, she left no itch unscratched and showed him every indulgence.
"The Living-Rope house's guard, Isogai Sensei, is a greater man than Hirate Miki at Sasagawa Shigezo's, whose name lives on in stories to this day."
notes: Speaker not named in the text; taken as O-Tetsu's boast to others, lifting Ryujiro as her house swordsman. Sensei kept for the irony.

payload.english: Lift him as high as they would, in truth it was no different from being locked in gaol.
"If I go on like this, I can never face Akioka Sensei."

His soul had not rotted through entirely. Unable to bear the pricks of conscience, he seized the opening he had at last found and, from the back garden of O-Tetsu's house, clinging to the wild grass, climbed down the cliff to the path between the rice fields in the valley.

Before he had time to think how glad he was, a snare fell from above with a snap. It caught him from under his left arm to over his right shoulder and, with a sharp tightening, he was fished straight up. His body hung in midair.
"Sensei, why do such a thing? Whatever happens, I shall never let you escape."
Above him O-Tetsu's voice, pitched high with rage, rang and rang.
III

O-Tetsu, returned by the narrowest chance, had stopped Ryujiro's flight with a ready thrown rope. She bound him up in a high-hands, small-hands tie and left him tumbled in the back loft, and beside him, gulping teacup sake in spite, she opened her mouth as if full of regret.
notes: Takade-kote rendered literally to keep the binding vocabulary; first-use gloss left to the catalogue passage.

payload.english: "Why, Sensei, did you try to run? In the little while I let my watch slip... And I had not gone out on other business either. From the pool at Sugatsu I went to fetch sesame eels to give you whole-boiled and put a little strength into you, and that from my own single heart, without leaving it to other hands. And to think of this."
O-Tetsu was even in tears.

payload.say: Drafted p45 to p53 in brisk kodan voice, keeping the dream plea and master-disciple language literal.

payload.english: Bound and left to lie as he was, Ryujiro was sickened by his own spiritlessness. He was sick of himself. This was all his punishment for betraying his master. For having fallen. Repenting in this way,
notes: Fragmentary judgment in the original; kept as short flat sentences rather than smoothing into one moral reflection.

payload.english: "Anego, forgive me, do. Whatever comes, I must make one journey to Edo and back."
notes: Kept Anego, Ryujiro's placating address to O-Tetsu as senior woman and boss, rather than sister.

payload.english: "Are you weary of this deep grass country? Or have you grown weary of me, that you tried to run away?"
"It is by no means that. I will go and see, and when my mind is at ease I will come straight back. The truth is, a dream every night troubles me and troubles me till I cannot bear it."
"A dream?"

"They say a dream is the weariness of the five viscera. Say that and there is an end of it, but one same dream repeated again and again will not leave my mind. It is my honoured master Akioka Jinpusai, in a dying state and near death. Now my master has not one kinsman. There can be no one to nurse him. He lives alone, and with his temper, which is peculiar, for a disciple he holds none but this Ryujiro here. That special training of one master and one disciple, that he will grant me the secret of the Happo Makigumo, I told you of it the other day."
notes: Kept five viscera literal for the period commonplace; kept Happo Makigumo untranslated as school secret to be held consistent.

payload.english: "That I have heard for certain."

"Should I fail to be in time before my master passes away, the hard-won secret will perish and, to my grief, will not remain in this world. That I cannot bear to lose. And apart from that too, in these days when duty and feeling have grown so thin, if I let my honoured master die alone as if uncared for, Isogai Ryujiro could not hold up his face. When the bond of master and disciple has become as if it were a business bargain, and I am full of dissatisfaction at it, I would by all means go and nurse my master..."
notes: Kept business bargain literal; this master-disciple rebuke is a load-bearing motif mirrored later by Kotora.

payload.english: "Is your master truly ill?"

payload.say: Drafted Ryujiro's plea, untying, and promise to return.

payload.english: "I do not know. But night after night I see it in dreams. It weighs on me till I cannot bear it. Please, sister, let me go to Edo once. I do not ask you to let me return to Edo for good. Only let me go. If my master is safe, I will come straight back here. If the dream is true and he is ill, I will nurse him, and after that I will surely return. I swear it solemnly."
notes: 金打致して誓い申す is an oath formula I could not settle literally; I have rendered it as a solemn vow rather than invent a rite. Ryujiro's 姉御 to O-Tetsu rendered as sister throughout.

payload.english: His sincerity rose to Ryujiro's eyes and stood there as tears. Even Living-Rope O-Tetsu could not but be moved. The complete expression of a human being's sincerity does not always need many words.

"If that is all, you need not have kept it from me and run off by the back garden. I am not a mere common woman, you know. If the reason runs straight, I will send you off in good cheer." She was surprisingly quick to understand. And at once she untied Ryujiro's bonds and stroked the marks where the rope had bitten, to bring the blood back into them.
notes: Kept bonds and rope literal for the binding web; 縄の喰入った痕 stroked 血の通うように is stroking to restore circulation.

payload.english: "I apologise to you many times over, but this morning my master weighed on my mind more than ever, and I felt as if I were racing the moments... I felt that by the difference of one step I might miss my master's last hour, and so without waiting for your return, sister, I rushed out. Pray do not think ill of me..."
So saying, Ryujiro timidly stretched his arms and legs.
notes: He has just been untied; the stretching is testing freed limbs, not exercise.

payload.english: "Oh, once the reason is clear, the rest is clean away. I think nothing of it. But, Sensei, you will truly come back to me, will you not?"
notes: Kept Sensei for O-Tetsu to Ryujiro to hold the house-swordsman irony.

payload.english: "I will surely return."

payload.say: Drafted the Mito-prophecy bargain and jealous warning at full length without softening either side.

payload.english: "As I told you with all my heart the other night, when Fujita Sensei of Mito was still living I heard this from him: before long the world will turn clean upside down and change till you are startled. So samurai, and hatamoto men above all, must think hard about their course, and for the most part they should set aside swordsmanship and spearmanship and that sort of thing and do better to study gunnery. And for that, he said, it is best to go once to the land of the red-haired foreigners... To tell the truth, I am of a mind to have you cross over to America, or to Holland. Forgive me for speaking of money, but we have laid by since my grandfather's day, and two or three thousand in gold I can make ready at any time."
notes: 'Two or three thousand in gold' keeps the original's bare 金, which names no coin; the sum is O-Tetsu's hoarded house money from her grandfather. 'Red-haired foreigners' renders 毛唐人 at its period level.

payload.english: "As to going abroad, there is the national ban, and there is Yoshida Shoin's failure, but by and by going will become possible, and I would by all means cross to a foreign land once, broaden my seeing and hearing, and receive instruction in gunnery and the like. As I must borrow your strength for it, I will surely return here."
notes: Ryujiro concedes the ban and the Shoin precedent, then turns them into a reason he must come back to O-Tetsu for her money.

payload.english: "And one thing more I will press upon you. Though you go back to Edo after so long, woman or no woman, whatever woman she may be — if you grow close with any, I shall not abide it."
She stored a fierce jealousy through the whole of that corpulent body — that was Living-Rope O-Tetsu.

payload.say: Page drafted in brisk kodan voice, keeping the outfit catalogue and ill-fortune meditation at full length.

payload.english: IV
O-Tetsu saw to his travelling dress down to the last thing and sent him off in the best of humour.

A plain iron-grey travelling half-cape, a hilt-bag of blue woollen cloth, wrist-covers and leggings of pale yellow Kai silk, a first-lined kimono in hailstone pattern worn short at the hem, no hakama, only an iron fan in his hand. So dressed, Ryujiro's fine manly figure shone all the more.
notes: Garment names are rendered as plain description rather than glossed Japanese terms; hakama and iron fan are left as in the house style for swordsman dress.

payload.english: "See you do not fall in with any woman on the way. Will you promise me that. My kobun are everywhere, you know. They will be watching you proper."
notes: Keeps O-Tetsu's cajoling command and her kobun surveillance warning literal.

payload.english: "Have no fear. Now I think only of my master's state, and next of yourself."
Ryujiro left her pleased with that, and pressed onward with all haste. Over the Fukuda upland and out to Ichizaki was but a breath.
Though now a free man, he could not shake the feeling that something strong still pulled him by the hair from behind. By it he knew how matchlessly O-Tetsu's power had pressed upon him till now.
notes: The hair-pulled-from-behind image is kept literal; it carries the invisible-rope binding without adding the word rope.

payload.english: By degrees the feeling grew upon him, as of a hooked fish out of the creel and swimming in the great river again. Now he was being drawn toward Edo.
"To my master, a moment the sooner."

His master Jinpusai was in truth a man dogged by ill fortune. The more he thought of it the more pitiable it seemed. Set beside such fencing masters as Saito Yakuro, Chiba Shusaku and Momoi Shunzo, his skill was in nothing inferior. Yet while the others took disciples by the thousand and were patronised by the shogunate or the lords, Akioka Jinpusai lived on in poverty in a ronin's lodgings, with in truth but a single disciple, himself. There, however, lay his greatness. He may have hidden himself of purpose in such a fate, but in any case the debt must be repaid in full.
notes: Keeps the three fashionable masters as a full list and the single-disciple poverty as the point of the passage, without ennobling or explaining it away.

payload.say: Drafted the roadside encounter with Kotora in brisk kodan English.

payload.english: For suffering himself to be detained on the road by O-Tetsu and breaking off his discipline of the sacred sword before the gods, for that fault he would apologize to the utmost. He would consult him too about going abroad to study gunnery. But praying that his master did not lie gravely ill as his dreams had shown him, he hastened his steps at every turn.

His plan was to go from Fukawa to Fussa, and thence by way of Nakabyo to Abiko, so from Ichizaki he hurried on by cut-through paths between fields and paddies by way of Shiizukashita. When the woods of Tatsuki on Monmadai had come close into view, he became aware that a young girl was following behind him.
She was by no means to be taken for a common farmer's daughter. Her hair was newly dressed in a bunkin high shimada, without a single hair astray.
notes: Kept bunkin-takashimada as a period coiffure term; a formal high shimada worn by young women and performers.

payload.english: From white powder to lip rouge, her heavy make-up was complete in every point. Even without it she was beautiful enough to make one shiver, a beauty rare even in Edo.

And yet, what was to be made of her dress. Her dyed yukata scattered with butterflies was all stained with dirt. With its large white ground, though it was still early autumn, it looked chill and shabby. Her obi too was narrow and all creased, wretched beyond words. Against the dressing of her hair and the painting of her face, her attire was all too mean, and the two did not accord at all. She must have been a riddle to any eye.
Stranger still, in this fine weather she carried a dark blue janome umbrella. And yet barefoot in straw sandals, she came stepping softly down the road.
notes: janome: a bull's-eye-patterned oil-paper umbrella.

payload.english: Could it be a fox of Onabakehara turned into a girl and following to bewitch him. To change shape even by day, it must be a fox of uncommon rank, he was half minded to jest to himself.
notes: Onabakehara is kept as a place-name; kanroku, literally official stipend, is taken as rank or power as a fox.

payload.english: When he hurried she hurried, when he rested she rested. She followed him like a shadow. When he looked back, she only smiled back at him. Ryujiro began to feel an unease.
"You are bound for Edo, samurai sir, are you not?"
notes: 御武家様 is a polite performer's address to a samurai gentleman; rendered to keep her formal sweetness.

payload.english: Out among the narrow paths of the rice fields, near where the stream runs in, she at last called out to him from behind.
notes: 流れ灌頂の有る辺: meaning uncertain; taken as an irrigation inlet where water runs into the paddies. Left as a plain landscape mark.

payload.english: "Yes," was all Ryujiro answered, and said nothing more.
"I too am bound for Edo," the girl said, unasked.
"Is that so," Ryujiro answered, curt as before.
"Will you lodge tonight at Fussa, or will you push on as far as Abiko?"

If he named a lodging she looked ready to ask to share it. Ryujiro could not help being on his guard. Even without his promise to O-Tetsu, he had no wish to grow close to this girl. Beautiful as she was, she was a woman of doubtful origin. There was no telling what trouble might come of it.
"No, I travel by night. It is to visit one gravely ill. I may take a fast palanquin, as need requires. In any case I go to Edo through the night," he answered. That, he thought, would silence her.
"Oh, is that so. I too have one gravely ill, and so I had thought to go through the night."
"You mean to travel the night road, and you a woman?"
"Yes, there is no help for it... If Danna-sama travels by night, nothing could give me more courage. I will follow behind you, so as not to be a burden."
notes: Kept Danna-sama per bible as Kotora's polite address to Ryujiro.

payload.english: "As you please."

She said she would only follow behind him, and there was no way to stop her. Troublesome as he found it, it could not be helped. And those words, to visit one gravely ill, struck a note somewhere in Ryujiro's heart.
"Who is it that is ill?" he found himself asking, before he knew it.
"It is only that I kept dreaming that our grand-master lay gravely ill, night after night, until I could bear it no longer, and so I alone slipped out and came away like this."
"What! A dream that your grand-master is ill--"
Ryujiro could not help starting.
V

In an age of poor roads, fearing for the safety of those cut off from one presses deeper than it does now. In a world with no telegraph, no telephone, no post, the mind by itself runs to imagining. And with that, superstition cannot help but run high.

A diviner's words. A dream. A crow's cry. Even a broken sandal-thong is feared as an evil omen. And so to set out from afar to visit the sick, taking a bad dream as if it were fact, is by no means rash or heedless.
notes: Crow's cry renders karasutobi/karasu naki phrasing; the sense is a crow's call taken as omen, not certain of the exact form.

payload.english: Ryujiro himself was bound for Edo on account of just such a dream, so he harboured no doubt of the girl. And at their being in the same plight, a sudden fellow feeling came over him.
"And that grand-master is--" Ryujiro asked, hastening onward all the while, of course.

"I am a travelling acrobat, one of the Takewari troupe, and I am called Kotora. The master I walk the circuits with is Takewari Toramatsu, and his master again is Takewari Toradayu, the grand-master of our art," the girl told her story for the first time.
"Ho, I had heard of the Takewari troupe."

payload.say: Drafted p107-p112 with Kotora's flight explained and the party hurried toward the Shin-Tone crossing.

payload.english: "Toradayu is stricken with palsy and has long lain abed in Hinomi Lane at Honjo Ishihara, but I am a foundling the grand-master picked up, and I have never known my true parents. To me the grand-master and his wife are the same as my own born parents. His wife died some years ago, so now the grand-master is all alone, but our present master Toramatsu, though his own son, is close-fisted and does nothing at all for the grand-master, and I pity him all the more for it. These bad dreams went on and on, and though I would go back to Edo to nurse him, Toramatsu is not a man to let me go for such a thing, so I slipped away in secret. From our engagement at Edosaki this way round may lose distance, but it suits me for hiding my tracks."
notes: chuki rendered as stricken with palsy; jishin/shin no oya nuance kept as same as my own born parents; jaken as close-fisted

payload.english: With this tale of Kotora's, every doubt was resolved. The mismatch between her hair and her dress, too, was nodded at as a thing that might well be, for a runaway performer.

"Ah, I too am anxious in the same way for my master in swordsmanship. In any case let us both hurry. An autumn day falls like a bucket into a well, as they say. It grows dark early, and at least the crossing from Fukawa to Fussa over the Hon-Tone must be got over while it is still light."
notes: tsurube-otoshi kept as proverbial simile; sessha rendered plainly as I

payload.english: "Hereabouts is all water. Marsh or river or cut channel, whichever way you go there is nothing but wet ground, and before the Hon-Tone there is still the Shin-Tone ferry to cross."
"Oh, the Shin-Tone ferry is just ahead now."
The Shin-Tone was cut in the Kanbun years from the Kokai River to Hirasu Marsh, a new channel fifty ken wide. It lay across the foot of the Tatsuki upland.
notes: Kanbun years left as period name; fifty ken kept as in text

payload.english: Before long the two came out at the landing. It was a truly desolate place. Below the upland stood a poor farmhouse here and there, but along the Shin-Tone itself not a single house, only reeds and river willows growing thick, and those not yet withered, which made it oppressively gloomy.

There is no ferryman at this crossing, only a boat kept ready, what they call a hand-hauled ferry. On either bank three timbers are set up high in a tripod, with a twisted wisteria-vine cable stretched between them, and over the cable is slipped a small ring of wire, and to that ring a cord is tied and made fast to the bow of a field boat. To bow and stern of the field boat besides, long hemp ropes are tied, each long enough to reach to either bank. That is to say, a man riding in the boat hauls in the bow rope himself and so reaches the far bank. When the next man comes after and wants to call the empty boat back to this side, he hauls in the stern rope from the bank and the boat comes back, though there is no one in it, a most primitive contrivance.
notes: Kept the mechanism at full length as performed explanation. 藤蔓 as wisteria-vine cable, 綱 as cord, 麻縄 as hemp rope to keep the rope web distinct. Final 房って来る read as 戻って来る, return.

payload.english: "They say it makes a great difference to the distance whether you get across by this ferry or not," Ryujiro said.
"As ill luck will have it the boat is lying at the far bank, but it will come back to this side if we only haul the rope," Kotora said, for she knew the place.

"The hemp ropes here, I hear, are presented by the house of Jinemon in Awa, where I was taken in, old capture-ropes given generation after generation. That house uses choice hemp from Hozoji in Mikawa, vinegar-boiled and laid threefold, and sure enough this is tougher stuff than the common kind."
notes: Kept the donation of worn-out capture-ropes literal and as hearsay as in the original; it is the engine for the later ferry ropes. 三繰り taken as threefold laying.

payload.say: Drafted p118 to p130 keeping the rope web, ferry gear and vulgar priest literal.

payload.english: So saying, Ryujiro began to haul. Guilty men or no, that the capture-ropes which had bound men to rob them of their freedom should now serve as ferry ropes to help men on their way, there was something deeply pointed in it even as mere making use of waste.
"Here, let me haul."
Kotora offered to haul in his place.
"No, I will not have a woman spend her strength, and besides you must not wet your sleeves."
Ryujiro stopped her and kept hauling himself. Kotora lent a hand to it. The boat left the far bank and, empty as it was, came on seven or eight ken, sliding its ring along the creeper.
notes: ken: the old measure of about two yards, kept as in the earlier ferry passage

payload.english: VI

At that moment there suddenly appeared among the reeds of the far bank the figure of a great hulking priest. Mouse-grey temple servant's coat with a narrow white cotton sash tied in front and tucked up behind for work, a twisted headband round a shaven head, vulgarity past all outlandishness. In one hand he carried a bucket dripping with water, in the other he planted a long handled eel rake for a staff. A fallen priest past all breaking and ruin. Yet his eyebrows were thick and heavy, his gaze was sharp, and on his forehead there was even a crescent shaped sword scar.
notes: the text writes three-month shape, taken as a crescent moon scar

payload.english: He looked for all the world like Lu Zhishen the Flower Monk of the Water Margin.
"Damn you, a young buck and a young wench tangling together and fooling as you call the boat. Who the shit would let you have it."
Though the far bank lay fifty ken away, his muttering rang out as if taken in the hand, and in a moment he set down his bucket and with one hand gave a hard pull on the opposing bow rope.
Two against one were beaten in an instant, and the boat that had started out turned back.

"Ah, good priest, I beg you. We are racing a step to visit the sick. Whether we are in time for a deathbed or not is a grave matter for us both, so please let the boat come to this side," Ryujiro pleaded aloud.
"No good. Damn it."

Though with one hand, he pulled with all his strength. The evil priest gave a hard pull. The two pulled too, desperately, with all their might. For a while it became a tug-of-war contest of strength. The empty boat hung hesitating midway, but the moment the priest braced himself and strained, the stern rope snapped with a twang and the party of two lost. The boat was drawn clean to the far bank by the priest's hand. There was now no way to draw the empty boat back to this side.
"Serves you right. Now go the long way round. There is no ferry near here. That has eased my spleen. I feel fine now. Well, well, I must scratch up a few more eels or I shall not get my drink money."
notes: Monk's music-hall vulgarity kept blunt; no softening of the gloating.

payload.english: The evil priest picked up his bucket again and vanished abruptly into the reeds. What a merciless priest. He was a man who had left the world to save men, yet he plied his eel-rake and broke the precept against killing, which was lawless enough, and then he took away the boat of salvation that carries men to the other shore. Of what temple, what priest could he be. Hateful as the fellow was, Ryujiro ground his teeth with vexation. But with the channel of the Shin-Tone between them, there was nothing to be done.
notes: Kept the ferry / salvation pun in 'boat of salvation that carries men to the other shore' rather than resolving it to one sense.

payload.english: "Nothing for it now but to go roundabout to where there is another ferry. Tch, damnable priest," Ryujiro fumed.
"Danna-sama, do not worry. I will go and fetch the boat. Getting to the far bank is nothing to me," said Kotora, as if it were nothing.
notes: Kept Danna-sama per bible; speaker is Kotora, address to Ryujiro.

payload.english: "What! Go to the far bank to fetch the boat?"
"I am a woman acrobat, and luckily this creeper-rope is stretched from over there to over here, so if I go along it, it will be nothing at all."
notes: Fujizuru kept as creeper-rope to hold the rope web literal.

payload.english: "I see."

payload.say: Drafted the creeper-rope crossing at the Shin-Tone ferry.

payload.english: It was a feat beyond an ordinary person, but for Kotora the woman acrobat it was nothing at all. When she slipped away from the troupe she had feared the changeable autumn sky and snatched up the nearest umbrella to hand, and without knowing it that had proved useful here. With no extra music struck up while the star makes ready, and no flourish at all, she merely tucked up the skirts of her yukata. Her faded red to-chirimen waistcloth stood out against the muddied water of the new cut and the mud below the low bank with an unexpected beauty.
notes: "While the tayu makes ready, another tune" is a theatre convention for filling time; the sense is she makes no show of preparation.

payload.english: In a moment she had clambered to the top of the parent post of the hand-hauled boat.
"Be careful, it is dangerous," Ryujiro called up to her from below.

"I am quite all right," Kotora said, smartly opening her dark blue bull's-eye umbrella. What for an instant looked like blood spraying in all directions from the chirimen of her waistcloth was the red dragonflies that had been resting on the creeper-rope, startled into flight.
notes: The text gives the mis-seeing first and the correction second; kept in that order.

payload.english: Shin-Tone in name, it was a fifty-ken cut. She crossed the creeper-rope of the hand-hauled ferry with a tightrope walker's step. It was truly splendid, no different from an ordinary person walking along a high road.

The low evening sun struck slantwise and lit half of Kotora bright red. It was mirrored too on the dull face of the sluggish water. A Kotora above, a Kotora below: one person seen as two. Even her stained yukata seemed in that light to give off a glow, and all the more her stage-style bunkin takashimada and her painted, beautiful face, and Ryujiro could not but gaze entranced. He no longer feared she might fall halfway, only that she might finish the crossing by herself and hurry on ahead alone. That alone weighed on him.

payload.say: Drafted the creeper-rope fall and the monk's reappearance keeping rope and vulgar registers literal.

payload.english: Presently she had worked her tightrope walk to the halfway point. However high the creeper is stretched from bank to bank, at its middle a slack forms of itself and hangs close to the face of the water. With the weight of a person's body added, it all but dipped and threatened to sink. Even that Kotora passed with skill. The hard place was all but passed, just when one thought she might pause to draw a breath.
"Ah!"

Almost in the same instant as Kotora's sharp cry, the stoutly twisted creeper-rope snapped apart. With a fearful great splash of water Kotora fell into the Shin-Tone cut. Ryujiro's horror rose to its height.
notes: Kept creeper-rope literal for the rope web; ぷつり as a short snap.

payload.english: VII
"Fooling about, are you! I fixed it so you should not cross, and coming tightrope-walking to fetch the boat, damn you — serve you right!"
notes: Monk in vulgar bluster, as in bible.

payload.english: Between the riverside willows on the far bank, the same evil monk as before had reappeared at some unseen moment, an eel-splitting knife in his hand. The fierceness of the eyes with which he glared this way was beyond telling. It was this fellow beyond doubt who had cut the creeper.
"I can swim a little. I shall be quite all right."

So saying, Kotora cast away her umbrella and struck out in a breaststroke. Even in a stroke or two her mastery in the water could be seen, and Ryujiro, reassured, beckoned to her, "Come this way, at any rate..."
Seeing the woman could swim, the evil monk on the far bank flared into a rage fit to send steam from his very crown,
notes: Sentence runs on into the abuse quoted in p154, which is outside this page; left as a lead-in rather than closed off.

payload.say: Drafted the ferry weeds confrontation keeping the binding vocabulary and the monk-Kotora vulgar exchange blunt.

payload.english: "Hey, woman, do you know of the man-eating weeds of the New Cut? Once you fall in here that is the end of you. The weeds and the water-chestnuts entangle your hands and feet and you can move no way at all. Heh, even carp, even crucian carp, when they grow big they get entangled in the weeds and perish here, this is a haunted place. If you were crossing alone I would do no such mischief to you, but it gripes me that you are with a young man. So then, wench, die and be done with it... or will you ask me to save you? Beg me and I will put the boat out for you..." There was no telling how hateful he looked as he said it.
"What, you shit of a monk? Die though I may, I would never be saved by the likes of you. Here, like this, I can swim, I tell you. What are man-eating weeds to me?"
notes: Kotora drops polite feminine speech for coarse abuse here; kept blunt to match the monk's vulgar register.

payload.english: Kotora cut even a showy crawl stroke to prove it. But it lasted only a moment. What the monk had said proved true, and at once the tip of a long slender weed entangled her foot. It was slimy and uncanny, as if it were the hand of a demon, so that you might have doubted whether blood ran and a pulse beat even in the water weeds. Once caught in it there was already nothing to be done. Before she knew it the weeds had entangled both her hands, left and right. Waist and arms too, and slantwise from under the arm up over the shoulder, they entangled her thick and fast, weeds of a fearsome and evil nature.

Seeing this, Ryujiro could by no means leave her to die. But he could not help thinking of the man sent to fetch a mummy becoming a mummy himself. Even if he dived in from this side, by the time he reached the place where Kotora was drowning he was bound to be caught in the same man-eating weeds.
notes: Kept the Japanese proverb literal as the image fits the weeds.

payload.english: More than that, for the moment he was filled with hatred for the evil monk. Even as mischief there is a limit. Even as meddling it was carried too far. Mad or witless, whichever he was, if he himself dived in now there was no knowing what hindrance the man might do.
notes: Oka-yaki here is uncertain; taken as officious meddling or harassing interference, but I am not sure of the period sense.

payload.english: In a flash Ryujiro made up his mind.

payload.say: Drafted the weed-rescue page keeping the small knife and ganjigarame hold literal.

payload.english: "Ei!" With a swift move he threw with all his might, as one throws a dart. It was the little knife drawn from his sword. That it flew fifty ken was splendid in itself, and it struck true, standing upright in the brow of the evil monk as if engraving a holy white curl there.
notes: kozuka is the small utility knife housed in the sword-scabbard; the text says he "threw shuriken" with it. Byakugo is the white curl on a Buddha's brow. Fifty ken is kept as written.

payload.english: "Wah!" With a single cry he toppled backwards and vanished from this side. It was indescribably satisfying.
Ryujiro quickly stripped off his clothes. He stopped short of his wrist-guards and leggings. He thrust his small knife behind him into his loincloth and dived into the Shin-Tone channel.
notes: He keeps tekko and kyahan on and keeps only the small knife; the long sword is left behind on the bank.

payload.english: Five or six ken were nothing, but as he pushed on to ten and fourteen or fifteen ken, the growth of weeds was thicker than he had thought. They tangled his hands, they tangled his feet, and he was startled by the dreadful power in them. There was nothing for it but to think that the weeds and water-caltrops had spirits in them and were spitefully taking revenge. If this was hard for him naked, he thought, how hard swimming must be for Kotora in her clothes.
Quite literally floundering through the weeds, he pushed on another ken or two, but then he could get no further forward. He felt as if he had been caught in the ganjigarame hold of the main rope.
notes: Mozogaki mozogaki plays on mogaki, to struggle, with mo, weeds. Ganjigarame is kept as the named hold from the catalogue; hon-nawa is the main binding cord.

payload.english: "Oh, that's it!"
Ryujiro understood. Here he would at once apply the art of rope-escape and rope-cutting he had been taught by Living-Rope O-Tetsu. That, he thought, was the best plan.
He drew his small knife underwater. Swimming with one hand, he cut the water weeds clear with single-handed cuts. At once a way out opened.
Struggling hard and fighting the man-eating weeds, he at last got to Kotora's side.
"Oh, Danna-sama!"
notes: Kept Kotora's polite address to Ryujiro.

payload.english: By this time Kotora was utterly worn out. But she did not, like one who knows no swimming, make the dangerous mistake of suddenly clinging to her rescuer.

payload.say: Drafted the underwater cutting free and climb back to the bank in plain past tense k–dan prose.

payload.english: VIII
The weeds of every kind entangled about Kotora's whole body, and Ryujiro's hard labour to cut them away and free her from the water demon's captivity, were in truth no light business.
notes: Suiyo literally water demon: kept literal as in the catalogue of water terrors, not explained away.

payload.english: He had to swim with one hand. The small knife held in the other hand, being underwater, would not work as he wished. If his care slackened for a moment he might wound Kotora's body. To cut off even a single finger would be a grave matter.
"Do not panic. Bear it a little longer."
notes: Speaker unstated: taken as Ryujiro steadying Kotora, and himself, while he cuts; left unattributed as in the original.

payload.english: Carrying on a feat more perilous than the diver who takes the jewel from before the nose of the sleeping dragon, Ryujiro at last cut the water weeds away and set Kotora free.
notes: A familiar feat of daring, kept at its full length rather than smoothed down.

payload.english: "You have saved my life. I shall never forget this debt," Kotora said in thanks from the bottom of her heart.
notes: Inochi no oya, life parent, is the set phrase for one who has saved a life: given by sense, not by parts.

payload.english: "Never mind that. Let us get ashore as quickly as we can." Ryujiro took the lead, cutting away the hindering water weeds again as he swam back to the bank they had come from. He had already cut a good way through before, so this time it was very much easier.

So the two returned to the same bank. Ryujiro had left his clothes and his long sword there. Kotora, for her part, had not only no cut path through the man-eating weeds if she went on ahead, but she felt it wrong toward her benefactor to go on alone.
notes: Both turn back: his reason is the clothes and sword left behind, hers is the uncut weeds ahead and loyalty to her rescuer.

payload.english: Once on the bank, the two breathed again.

Ryujiro happened to look toward Kotora and was startled. From several places on her hands and legs dark blood was gushing out. He thought for a moment the point of his small knife had touched her and wounded her. But when he saw they were leeches sucking there, he was relieved.
notes: The blood is leeches, not a knife wound: left to resolve as in the original.

payload.english: "Come, we will cross no more at such a spiteful place. Even if we go round, let us go by another way," Ryujiro said.
"That will be best," Kotora said, wringing out her wet clothes as she spoke.
"Oh!"
notes: Exclamation left unattributed as in the original; the next paragraph shows it is Ryujiro on finding his clothes gone.

payload.say: Drafted the stripping on the bank flat and literal, with soul sword against little knife kept distinct.

payload.english: Ryujiro could not keep from crying out. And no wonder. The half coat he had cast off was gone, and with it the lined robe, the under-robe, even the sash. And not only those. The long sword he had left behind was gone, and everything besides, from the things in his breast to his hand towel and nose papers.
notes: Half coat, lined robe, under-robe and sash render han-gappa, awase, juban and obi; breast things, hand towel and nose papers render kaichu-mono, tenugui and hanagami. Left the catalogue complete as in the Japanese.

payload.english: "Who has taken them!"
Isogai Ryujiro had been stripped naked. Only his little knife was left to him, and even the long sword, the soul of the samurai, had been carried off by someone.
notes: Keeps the p2 phrase soul of the samurai literal, and keeps long sword against little knife distinct: daito left on the bank and stolen, kodachi kept in the loincloth.

payload.english: "Oh, it is because you saved me, sir, that you have been brought to this trouble. I have no excuse," Kotora herself turned pale as she said it.
notes: Sir renders danna-sama, Kotora's polite address to a samurai gentleman.

payload.english: "My mind was all on cutting weeds and I gave no thought to this side. When did it happen, and who did it?" Ryujiro raged, but there was nothing to be done.
Even the bell of a distant temple had begun to sound. With every blink the country round grew darker. A cold wind pressed upon the skin of the two.

"In any case, let us make for where there are houses, and dry your wet clothes, and put other hands to searching for my lost things. Someone may have seen the thief." So saying, Ryujiro went ahead through the reeds toward the foot of the Tatsuki terrace. Kotora followed behind him.

Apart from the guards on his hands and legs, Ryujiro was naked, with only the little knife stuck in his loincloth, a disgrace beyond disgrace. Strange calamity though it was, what a plight. All of it was rust bred from his own body, from disobeying his sword master's command and letting himself be detained by a woman boss and falling, against his will, into idle ways. That it should come to this was his own doing, and remorse pressed thick upon him.
notes: Guards on hands and legs render tekko kyahan, left on his body. Rust renders sabi in its moral sense, as self-earned corrosion, not literal rust.

payload.english: They went first into the nearest farmhouse below the terrace, but the house held to the custom of this land, to have nothing to do with travellers once night has fallen, and would not let them in past the threshold. Though they pleaded their case, no one would listen.

payload.say: Drafted the night refusal to O-Tetsu's reveal, keeping net and binding language literal.

payload.english: At the next house they shut the door in great haste, and call and knock as they might, there was no answer. They tried three or four other houses, and were turned away at them all.
At their wits' end, Ryujiro and Kotora went back to the ferry landing where they had started. Night had already fallen, and the evening moon was out.

"All of this comes from my own carelessness. At this rate, even if I returned to Edo, even if my master is alive and well, I could not for shame show my face. I must change my plan. Come, Kotora, what say you. Go on ahead and give no thought to me."
notes: Ryujiro's sessha rendered as plain I to keep his samurai formality without archaism.

payload.english: "How could I do such a thing?" Kotora's voice was in earnest.
"Forgive me, but I have a little money kept inside my belly band. Once we reach the town of Fukawa there will surely be a secondhand clothes shop. With the night to cover us, come, let us push on."
She took Ryujiro by the hand and made to walk along the edge of the channel.
"Wait a moment." It was a woman's voice from among the reeds. It was Living-Rope O-Tetsu.
IX
"It was I who took your clothes. Your swords and everything else, I have hidden them all away."
O-Tetsu roughly tore Ryujiro and Kotora apart and stood between them, roaring at them.
Kotora started and began to tremble. Ryujiro, once he knew it was O-Tetsu, could not speak a word. He was like a gnat stared down by a toad.
notes: Simile kept literal as written; no softening of Ryujiro's passivity.

payload.english: "I thought something of this sort would happen, so while you were getting yourself ready I sent my kobun running ahead along every road, to get our own people to spread a net in advance. And all the while I followed behind in disguise, and without ever knowing you were watched and followed, you fell in with this wench and walked the paths between the paddies as friendly as could be, all but tangled together. I was jealous enough even to envy the scarecrows that looked at you."
notes: Net and tangled kept literal to hold the binding web. The scarecrow clause is compressed in the Japanese; read as jealousy even of scarecrows that watched them.

payload.say: Drafted p207-p218 in brisk kodan voice, keeping jealous registers and the laid-aside knife literal.

payload.english: By O-Tetsu's own telling, the man set to watch this ferry was an old kobun of hers, Ahodara Gonji. A gambler by trade, and a sham monk.
notes: True identity revealed late here: the blocking monk of p124 was O-Tetsu's man all along. Kept romanisation as in bible.

payload.english: It was clear now too that the reason every farmhouse below the Tatsuki bluff had shut its doors to the two of them was that O-Tetsu's word had gone round.
"There, that is the reach I have. And yet you go trailing off on a lovers' road with a snivelling brat like this? A drenched wench and a naked man, there is nothing very stylish in that."
notes: O-Tetsu's jealous register: coarsening and possessive. Kept lovers' road for michiyuki/doubly-suicidal elopement sense without explaining.

payload.english: Against a heart burning with blind, sick jealousy, neither reason nor feeling could prevail.
"No, we two are nothing of that sort, neither fond nor anything," Ryujiro set about excusing himself.
"Mistress, please do not think ill of us," Kotora too tried to make her peace.
notes: Kotora addresses O-Tetsu as okami-san; rendered as Mistress to keep placating senior-woman sense in English.

payload.english: "Eh? What is this tadpole saying? What right have you to speak straight to a great boss like myself, woman though I am? Hold your tongue and get back," O-Tetsu suddenly thrust Kotora away.
notes: o-tamajakushi is literally tadpole, used as belittling brat. Kept literal.

payload.english: Kotora as she fell struck her side on an old stake and went sprawling. O-Tetsu with شع vindictive spite kicked her as she lay and even spat on her. Ryujiro felt at last he could no longer bear this ignorant bullying of O-Tetsu's. With this woman, he thought, he could never make anything of his life. And yet now there was nothing to be done.
"Well, I give up going to Edo. We will go back to Awa from here. There I will clear myself. In any case, my clothes," he said.
notes: Speaker unstated in Japanese; from context it is Ryujiro submitting.

payload.english: O-Tetsu's delight at this was beyond all measure.
"Here they are, see. I have them all safe. Come, you will catch cold. Put them on quickly."
She dressed him as a mother dresses a child fresh from the bath. That Ryujiro first drew the small knife from his loincloth and laid it by the roadside goes without saying.
notes: Kept the scale-comedy simile literal. The laying aside of the knife, stated as obvious, is what lets Kotora take it unseen in next paragraph.

payload.english: The fallen Kotora quietly took it. No sooner had she drawn it than she drove it suddenly into O-Tetsu's side. O-Tetsu's scream was a single cry.
notes: Kept flat as written: one cry, no death stated.

payload.english: "It is a woman's pride. I am Take-wari Kotora, after all. Come, Danna-sama, I shall go with you to Edo."
notes: Kept Danna-sama and troupe name as claimed identity; no build-up added.

payload.english: She wiped the bloodied blade on O-Tetsu's sleeve, put it back in its sheath, and handed it back to him.
What could never have been settled in one way or two was simply cut through by Kotora. Ryujiro could only marvel at the strangeness of fate.

Mr ○○○○○, famed until mid-Meiji as the Metropolitan Police's foremost old detective in arrests, was none other than the later self of this Isogai Ryujiro. His former wife was none other than Kotora, though she is said to have died of illness early in Meiji. Whether Ryujiro ever received the secret transmission of Happo Makigumo from Jinpusai, on that point, regrettably, nothing has come down.
notes: Kept circles and flat closing shrug as written; names in romanisation without addition.

payload.say: Part is plot-clear but English repeatedly slips into literal idiom, fragmentary description and agreement errors, with one corrupted string needing instant correction.
The part keeps the rope web, catalogue length and flat ending well, but needs fixes for idioms, term consistency and two misreadings.

Most notes were a reader catching something real and were taken in the smallest form: the double-sandal idiom at p7, 'taking men prisoner' at p9, rumour 'to be heard' at p10, the missing main verb at p15, single-heir transmission at p28, 'flatter him as they might' at p35, 'achieved his aim' at p4, the dangling night-boat opener at p13, the shoulder image at p31, 'anticipated his every want' at p33, the standardised high-hands/low-hands at p42 with 'out of spite ... full of vexation', 'as plain as if beside us' at p127, the reversed suspect/doubt at p156, the dart expansion cut at p160, the ganjigarame cross-lattice bind restored at p164, the corrupted characters removed at p214, the self-made rust idiom at p191, and the hair-pulled reluctance marked as a feeling at p71. Declined, with reasons the reader can follow: F9 (America/Holland kept; transliteration plus gloss would be expansion in O-Tetsu's speech), R7 and R8 (the verbless costume inventories keep the Japanese listing rhythm, and the suggested garment terms are unsettled), R9 (the was/were change breaks the staged mis-seeing), R10 (the Buddha's white curl stays literal; explanation belongs in the margin), R11 ('deeply pointed' keeps the narrator savouring 廃物利用), R14 ('rolled in the palm' keeps 円め込められて and the plaything comedy), R15 (the suggested wording is no less modern and repeats 'stomach'), R16 ('cut off' keeps 隔絶, the severance the dream-essay turns on), R18 (chirimen must stay one consistent term across p139 and p142), and R19 ('former wife' kept for 其前の妻女 in the flat coda). Two reader pairs overlapped rather than disagreed and were taken together: F8/R4 at p42 and F14/R1 at p214; at p156 F11 and R12 agreed on the sense and F11's 'suspected' was taken. One place goes up to the editor: the monk's abuse at p126, where the readable reader's 'Like hell I'd let you have it' is speakable but redirects the insult, and the literal 'Who the shit' is not speakable English — the reading fixes the level of vulgarity but not the English form. payload.say: Fixes made: the blade thrown at the monk (p160 "kozuka drawn from his sword") is now distinct from the small knife used underwater, since the Japanese has two different words (刀の小柄; 小刀) and the continuity of which blade Kotora later picks up depends on it; "as plain as if close at hand" (p127), Japanese 手に取るように, replaces "beside us", which invented a first-person narrator; "Guilty though the men they bound may have been" (p118) restores the concession in 罪有る者とは云え, which "Guilty men or no" reversed; "bunkin high shimada" (p144) now matches the same Japanese term's first rendering; "water-caltrops" (p154) now matches the 菱 rendering used a page later, so the man-eating weeds read as one plant; "Anego" (p54, p57) now matches the first rendering of 姉御 in this scene, so Ryūjirō's address to O-Tetsu does not change mid-conversation; and "handed down from master to master alone" (p4) restores 一家相伝, the one-master-to-one-disciple transmission the book's master-and-disciple theme turns on, where "his house" suggested a family line. The rope catalogues, the ferry mechanism, the dream essay, the rumour as rumour, the poison as suspicion, Kotora's flat stabbing with no death stated, and the circles and shrug of the coda are all as the Japanese leaves them.

chapter_summaries.0: 一: Ryūjirō readies to flee. Set-up: hatamoto swordsman on shrine-purification pilgrimage for Happō Makigumo transmission, beached three months at Awa by Living-Rope O-Tetsu, widowed oyabun with 1000 kobun and rumoured torture-murders of five-six men. Portrait of fortyish corpulent O-Tetsu; carrying on back, nursing, invisible sickness, decision to slip via back cliff to Fukuda.

hard_spots.why_hard: Two-paragraph incantatory list of rope arts (kakenawa, toinawa, hikinawa etc.) and holds (ganjigarame, kikkō, matsuba, rokuro-maki, takade, kote...) plus sō-returns in shin-gyō-sō variants. Tempts summarising; must be kept at full length because p164 later binds Ryūjirō 'exactly like a ganjigarame'. Requires consistent English set, not varied synonyms.

Full-paragraph kōdan explanation of hand-hauled ferry: tripods, creeper cable, iron ring, bow/stern hemp lines. Narrator pauses to savour it and adds donated retired capture-ropes from Hōzōji hemp. Do not move to footnote or compress into efficient summary.

Single-speech village rumour listing five-six dead captives with kirishitan-bateren joke and evil-eye paralysis. Delivers O-Tetsu's menace as hearsay, not fact. Keep as reported speech, not settled history.
Narrator's lecture that before telegraph/telephone/post, bad dreams and broken sandal-thongs were reason to cross provinces. Pulp sociology that licenses both escapes. Do not shrink to a sentence.

Sour-smelling cooled water and chopped surume lunch as possible poisoning. Text offers as retrospective evil surmise (邪推), never confirmed. English must keep as suspicion, not fact that O-Tetsu drugged him.

Rope biting into O-Tetsu's rich flesh as she slips free; faded red crepe loincloth against muddy water; blood-spray that is only red dragonflies. Linger at original level: neither veiled nor heated up.

Kozuka thrown 50 ken into monk's brow; Kotora's sudden side-stab of O-Tetsu, one scream, knife wiped on sleeve and returned. No remorse build-up, no confirmed death statement. Keep breath-short and deadpan.

Leap to mid-Meiji: famous First detective printed as circles ○○○○○ as Ryūjirō's later self, Kotora as dead first wife, and flat shrug whether Happō Makigumo secret was ever transmitted. Keep circles and shrug; do not explain or resolve.

part_summaries.summary: 一: Ryūjirō readies to flee. Set-up: hatamoto swordsman on shrine-purification pilgrimage for Happō Makigumo transmission, beached three months at Awa by Living-Rope O-Tetsu, widowed oyabun with 1000 kobun and rumoured torture-murders of five-six men. Portrait of fortyish corpulent O-Tetsu; carrying on back, nursing, invisible sickness, decision to slip via back cliff to Fukuda.

二: Conscience and backstory. Training under Imahori and sole pupil of rōnin Akioka Jinpūsai; pilgrimage order to shrines. Poison suspicion (surume, sour yuhashi). Hereditary mekashi house; midnight rope-lesson catalogue (holds and shin-gyō-sō variants), mutual tying, O-Tetsu slipping bonds. Flattered as house swordsman better than Hirate Miki; thrown-rope recapture from cliff.

三: Recapture and bargaining. Hog-tied in back upstairs while O-Tetsu drinks. Ryūjirō invents/ reports nightly dream of dying kinless master; pleads one Edo nursing visit on oath to return. O-Tetsu releases and strokes rope-marks, extracts promises: foreign gunnery voyage on hoarded thousands, and jealous ban on other women. Jealousy as stored bulk.

四: Send-off and new companion. O-Tetsu kits him out (michiyuki, tsuka-bukuro, tekko-kyahan) and warns kobun everywhere. Ryūjirō hurries via Fukuda-Ichizaki toward Fūkawa-Fussa-Abiko. Meets incongruous beauty: high coiffure and heavy makeup with shabby dyed yukata and rain umbrella, bare feet. She shadows him; both claim night road for sick masters.

五: Dream essay and Kotora's tale. Narrator lectures that without telegraph/post a bad dream justified crossing provinces. Girl is Take-wari Kotora, foundling of grand-master Toradayū (now paralysed in Honjo), fleeing miserly Toramatsu from Edosaki engagement. They hurry for Hontone crossing before dark; reach lonely Shin-Tone hand-hauled ferry and begin hauling.

六: Ferry blocked. Giant fallen monk (earth-coloured nasshogi, twisted headband, sword scar) hauls opposite rope one-handed, wins tug, stern line snaps. He jeers, hides for eels. Kotora offers tightrope on creeper via umbrella; red loincloth flash, dragonflies like blood-spray, sunset double on water. Midway creeper snaps; she falls with loud splash.

七: Water rescue. Monk reappears with eel-knife, boasts he cut vine, taunts about man-eating weeds/algae. Kotora swims then is seized hand-foot-side-shoulder like living hands. Ryūjirō throws kozuka 50 ken into monk's brow, strips to tekko-kyahan and loincloth dirk, swims, finds weeds like ganjigarame, cuts free with O-Tetsu's rope-cutting method.

八: Naked robbery. Ryūjirō cuts weeds one-handed while guarding blade near Kotora, swims back to same bank. Leeches mistaken for knife wounds. Clothes, two swords, pocket things, towel and nose-paper gone. Farmhouses refuse lodging at night rule. They return to ferry under evening moon; Ryūjirō tells Kotora go on alone; she refuses, offers belly-band savings for secondhand clothes in Fūkawa.

九 + coda: O-Tetsu springs from reeds, owns theft via forward net of kobun, reveals monk as old kobun Ahodara Gonji and farmers silenced. Jealous rage beats and spits on Kotora. Ryūjirō gives up Edo trip to prove innocence; while mother-dressing him she is side-stabbed by Kotora with his dirk — one scream, woman's pride, knife wiped and returned. Asterisks: Ryūjirō as Meiji's First detective ○○○○○, Kotora dead first wife; whether secret transmitted unknown.

bible.say: Rope is plot, not colour: keep catalogues full and binding-words literal; keep hero passive, O-Tetsu unglamorous-menacing, Kotora polite then abrupt, ending flat. Where passage contradicts this bible, passage wins — say so.

style_sheet.annotation_density: Sparse, for what sentence cannot give: torinawa arts, jitte / aka-fusa, Shin-Tone / Hontone geography, kirishitan-bateren joke, Mito prophecy, circles redaction. Never for what context supplies. Margin explains choices; text wins over reader ease.
style_sheet.author_voice: Brisk magazine kōdan under bookish Sinitic ornament: formal de-aru narration, performed rumour, lingering erotic-comic body description, deadpan anticlimax. Neither faux-Edo pastiche nor sleek modern flat. Keep scale comedy (carried like child, dressed after bath) and failing body (pallor, sunken eyes, grown topknot) plain.
style_sheet.honorifics_and_names: Japanese order surname-first; macrons (Ryūjirō, Jinpūsai, Toradayū). Keep Sensei for Akioka where pupil-duty weight matters; keep O- prefix (O-Tetsu, not Tetsu). 先生 addressed to Ryūjirō as 'Sensei' to keep house-swordsman irony. Danna-sama for Kotora's address. No -san/-sama beyond what English needs.
style_sheet.keep_in_japanese: Sensei, hatamoto, kobun, jitte, torinawa/kakenawa etc. with first-use gloss; place-names in romanisation (Awa, Shin-Tone, Tatsuki). Named holds in consistent English with Japanese first time (e.g. ganjigarame cross-lattice bind) then English alone.
style_sheet.quotation: Dialogue in double quotes; rumour speech and reported injunctions as quoted blocks where original sets them as performance. Keep who-said-what spare as original leaves it.
style_sheet.register: Narration literate-formal but brisk; dialogue sharply differentiated: Ryūjirō samurai-formal self-abasing, O-Tetsu cajoling-commanding-jealous, Kotora polite-feminine snapping to vulgar then flat, monk music-hall vulgar.
style_sheet.ruby_and_italics: Ruby readings (e.g. 磯貝竜次郎いそがいりゅうじろう) do not appear in English; use romanised name. Italics only for coda circles ○○○○○ and for blood-spray/dragonfly feint if needed. No italics for Japanese terms after first gloss.

crux.for_the_english: Keep the ropes literal. Give the named holds and techniques in a consistent, recognisable set of English terms, and let the catalogue run at its full, slightly excessive length the first time: it is plot, not ornament, because the algae will later bind him 'exactly like a ganjigarame hold'. Do not vary rope, bind, tie, entangle, prisoner for elegance; the text's network of repeated binding-words is its structure, and flattening it is destroying that network.
crux.point: The story stands or falls on its title made literal: the sword fails and the rope, in every form, does everything. Ryūjirō's great sword, the 'soul of the samurai', is stolen off a riverbank while he is naked; his small knife is useful only once, thrown at a man and then used as a weed-cutter. What actually saves a life, twice, is the low, female, criminal-adjacent art he learned in captivity from O-Tetsu: rope-escape and rope-cutting, applied underwater to the man-eating weeds that hold Kotora. Around that core the text binds everything to everything else — the invisible rope that keeps him in Awa for three months, the thrown rope that fishes him off the cliff, the ferry's hauling-ropes (themselves donated, used-up capture-ropes, a detail the narrator pauses to savour), the weeds that climb his body 'like a real rope-hold', the jealousy that is also a kind of tying. A translation that treats the rope business as colour, cuts the catalogues, or lets the swordsmanship reassert heroic dignity has lost the book's actual engine, which is a proud hatamoto swordsman being progressively stripped — of movement, of clothes, of his sword, of initiative — and rescued, bound, dressed and finally freed by women.
crux.why: Because the plot is built as a chain of bindings and releases, and because Ryūjirō's passivity is the point, not a flaw to be tidied. He is carried on O-Tetsu's back, nursed, kept, flattered as a house swordsman 'better than Hirate Mikizō', caught mid-escape like a fish on a line; he apologises, weeps, promises, undresses, and is dressed again by O-Tetsu 'like a mother after a child's bath'. Kotora walks the rope he cannot, swims, is cut free by his borrowed skill, and then settles the whole impasse in one stab while he stands by astonished at fate. If the English lets him sound decisive or lets O-Tetsu become a glamorous villainess, the humiliation-comedy and the real menace both go.

reading.head_on_cruxes: Fork opened because the first parts do name the same rope-over-sword structure, but Option 1 names a materially different second crux about pulp abruptness and refusal to resolve, which Option 0 does not; that difference will drive recurring choices about clarification, moral build-up and the epilogue, and getting its status wrong would be expensive across the text.

open_questions.question: Was Ryūjirō actually poisoned or dosed — the sour-smelling cooled water on the boat, the food-poisoning he half-rejects as an explanation — or is this his retrospective suspicion, and does the text ever settle it? It does not; keep the suspicion as suspicion and do not let the English imply O-Tetsu drugged him.
open_questions.why_it_matters: It decides whether O-Tetsu is a near-supernatural 'demon' of the rumours in p9 or a formidably competent woman whose nursing, watching and rope-work are quite enough. The opening calls her a yōma on hearsay; the narrative never confirms anything uncanny.

open_questions.question: Is O-Tetsu dead? Kotora stabs her in the side, she screams once, and the text moves on within two sentences to 'fate is strange'; no death is stated. How flatly should the English leave that?
open_questions.why_it_matters: A translation that writes 'killed her' tidies what the original elides; one that softens it to a wound invents mercy. The brutal casualness is characteristic and should stay visible as an open question for the editor.

open_questions.question: The closing redaction '○○○○○' for the famous Meiji detective, and the admission that nobody knows whether Ryūjirō ever received the Happō Makigumo secret: keep the circles and the shrug exactly?
open_questions.why_it_matters: This coda deflates the whole quest — the transmission the story was launched by is simply 'not handed down'. Annotating a guessed name or resolving the question would betray the ending's deliberate anticlimax.

open_questions.question: Are the matching dreams (his master dying, her grand-master dying) meant as genuine presentiment in a pre-telegraph world, as the narrator's essay at p101–102 insists such anxiety was, or as convenient pretexts both escapees half-believe?
open_questions.why_it_matters: It governs tone in the long plea scene: played straight, Ryūjirō's tears and Kinchō oath are sincere period piety about master-and-disciple; played with irony the scene becomes two runaways recognising a fellow-feeling. The narrator seems to endorse the period logic; recommend keeping that endorsement un-ironic.

reading.reading:
The crux is the rope, and everything else in this 1925 kōdan-magazine story hangs off it. Ryūjirō leaves Edo on a pilgrim's progress of shrines to purify himself before receiving the secret transmission of the Happō Makigumo school; he is beached instead at Awa by O-Tetsu — 'Ikina no O-Tetsu', Living-Rope O-Tetsu — a widowed, corpulent, near-forty female oyabun who holds a dead husband's red-tasselled jitte, commands a thousand kobun across the Tone, and is rumoured to have tortured five or six captive men to death. Three months of luxurious imprisonment follow, during which the bored prisoner studies her family's hereditary capture-rope manuals and takes midnight practical lessons, each tying the other up. That tuition, not his sword, is what the story is stockpiling: at the Shin-Tone ferry the villainous fake monk cuts the creeper-rope under Kotora, the weeds take her, and Ryūjirō cuts them both free with a small knife using exactly what O-Tetsu taught him. The translation must therefore keep the technical rope vocabulary — kakenawa, hikinawa, the ganjigarame, kikkō, matsuba and the rest, in their shin-gyō-sō variants — patiently and consistently, and resist impoverishment into generic 'knots and ties'. The catalogue at p25–26 will tempt any fluent draft to summarise; summarising is the single most damaging cut available, because the later underwater fight is written as that catalogue come alive.

The second thing to hold is the narrator. This is popular Taishō storytelling in formal de-aru narration, and the narrator constantly steps forward: to give rumour as a set-piece speech (p9), to explain the hauling-ferry's mechanism for a full paragraph of tripods, creeper cable and iron ring (p114), to lecture on how, before telegraph or post, a bad dream was reason enough to cross provinces (p101–102), and finally to leap half a century to Meiji and a famous detective whose name is printed as circles. None of this is padding to a kōdan reader; it is the pleasure of the form — digression, explanation and anticlimax delivered with a straight face. Do not rationalise the chronology, do not move the explanations into footnotes where the original performs them in the voice, and do not warm or darken the ending: Kotora's murder of O-Tetsu is dispatched in a breath, and the coda ('whether he received the secret transmission is, regrettably, not known') must stay as flat as it is. A fluent version will instinctively ennoble — make the prose sleeker, the hero worthier, the jealous older woman more tragic, the stabbing more consequential. Every one of those instincts is a deformation here.

Register needs care in both directions. The narration is literate, even bookish, full of period and Sinitic colour, but it is magazine prose, brisk under the ornament; archaising it into faux-Edo pastiche would be as wrong as modernising it flat. Dialogue does the social work and must stay differentiated: Ryūjirō's samurai formality and self-abasement, O-Tetsu's mixing of wifely cajoling, oyabun command and obscene jealousy, Kotora's polite performer's femininity that can snap into 'you shit of a monk' defiance mid-river (p155) and a flat 'it's a woman's honour' over a bloody knife (p220), the monk's music-hall vulgarity. The comedy and the erotic undertow — the lessons at midnight, the rope biting into O-Tetsu's rich flesh as she writhes free (p31), the faded red crepe loincloth glimpsed against the mud (p139), Ryūjirō naked but for leggings and a knife in his loincloth — should be translated at the original's own level of lingering: neither prudishly veiled nor heated up. Note the physical comedy of scale: she carries him half a ri on her back 'as if he were a child'; he is dressed by her like one. Keep his body failing — pallor, sunken eyes, grown-out topknot — as plainly as her twenty-kan bulk, double chin and charm are kept in the long appraising portrait at p11, which sizes her up as a woman past bloom who might once have moved men; translate that appraisal without either leering or rescuing her from it.

What the text leans on, besides rope, is water and masters. Rivers, ferries, weeds, leeches, eels and eel-catching monks saturate the middle chapters; two dying masters, one for each runaway, mirror each other and license both escapes, and the master-disciple ethic is argued aloud at length (p50–54) as a rebuke to an age when the bond has become 'like a business transaction'. The foreign thread — Fujita's Mito prophecy of the world turned upside down, gunnery, America or Holland on her grandfather's hoarded thousands — is not decoration either: it is O-Tetsu's own escape-plan for him, and one of the promises that binds him to return. Likely fluent errors, to be named plainly: cutting or compressing the rope catalogues and the ferry mechanism; varying the binding vocabulary; clarifying the poison suspicion into fact; adding remorse, hesitation or heroism to Ryūjirō; making Kotora's stab reluctant or O-Tetsu's death explicit and mourned; explaining the leeches, the circles in the coda, or the lily-like final shrug; and letting the dream-essay shrink into a sentence. Where the English must choose, choose the rope, the digression, and the flat ending.
reading.say: 'I think this is wrong, though I'm not sure, and here's why' is worth more than a confident guess; 'none' is a complete answer. Never invent a source or a reading to fill a gap; leave the gap visible. (From the house brief, as reminder to the translator.)

second_crux.for_the_english: Keep one audible lexical web — rope, cord, bind, tie, tangle, coil, haul, cut loose, escape — recurring even where idiomatic English would vary it, and keep the technical catalogues of knots and holds at full, incantatory length. Likewise let the swords stay inert: never drawn in combat, finally stolen while he is naked; do not heroicise Ryuujirou into a swordsman in action.
second_crux.point: The whole story is organised by rope displacing the sword, literally and metaphorically — this is what the title announces and what every episode re-enacts.
second_crux.why: Otetsu is Ikina wa, 'Living Rope': a bondage/arrest-rope (torinawa) expert whose house transmits knot-lists (ganjigarame, kikkou, matsuba, rokuro…) that Ryuujirou studies by being tied and tying her in midnight lessons. He is then held three months by an 'invisible rope' though never locked in, is hauled back by her thrown rope when he escapes, crosses paths with the ferry's hauling-ropes (made, pointedly, from retired arrest-ropes), watches Kotora tightrope the ferry vine, is nearly drowned by man-eating algae that binds him 'like a ganjigarame', and frees himself and her only by applying Otetsu's rope-escape/rope-cutting teaching with his small knife. Even Otetsu's jealous surveillance is described as a net spread along the road. Against this, the samurai's daishou do nothing: the long sword is left on the bank and stolen, and the only blades that work are the kozuka thrown at the monk and the kodachi cutting weeds in the water.

second_crux.for_the_english: Preserve the sensational, deadpan narration and its refusals: do not clarify who is villain or victim, do not soften the bondage's erotic charge or the jealous violence, do not give the stabbing a moral build-up it doesn't have, and do not fill the epilogue's gap about the secret transmission. Where a fluent version would explain or resolve, leave the seam showing.
second_crux.point: The ending's moral and narrative abruptness is deliberate pulp mechanics, not a flaw to be repaired: the captive's problem is 'solved' by a near-stranger's sudden murder, and the frame then leaps to Meiji and openly admits it doesn't know the outcome that mattered most.
